q: Why do some people have such vivid dreams while others remember nothing?
Why do some people remember their dreams and others don't?
Why can some people not remember their dreams?
Why do some people dream more than others?
What determines if you remember dreams?
a: Dream recall varies dramatically between individuals due to several biological and psychological factors. People who wake up during or immediately after REM sleep are more likely to remember their dreams, while those who wake up during deep non-REM sleep rarely recall dreams. The brain region responsible for forming new memories (the hippocampus) is less active during REM sleep, which is why most dreams are forgotten. Some people have a genetic predisposition to better dream recall, possibly linked to higher activity in the prefrontal cortex during REM sleep. Personality traits also play a role: people who are more anxious, open to new experiences, or have higher creativity tend to remember dreams more frequently. Stress, certain medications, and sleep disorders can increase dream intensity and recall. Age is another factor — children have more vivid and frequent dreams, while dream recall decreases with age. Some people simply don't pay attention to or prioritize remembering their dreams, while others keep dream journals that train their brains to retain dream content. The neurotransmitter acetylcholine, which is elevated during REM sleep, may also influence dream vividness.

Dreams occur primarily during REM (Rapid Eye Movement) sleep when brain activity is similar to wakefulness. The brainstem triggers REM sleep, activating neurotransmitters like acetylcholine while suppressing others. Dreams are thought to help with memory consolidation, emotional processing, and problem-solving. Dream recall varies between individuals due to genetics, personality, sleep patterns, and attention to dreams.
